paragraphs.heading: The physics of the very small
paragraphs.text: Quantum mechanics, also called quantum physics, is the basic theory of how matter and light behave. The behaviour it describes usually happens at the scale of atoms and below, and it is often called counterintuitive. Classical physics describes much of nature at everyday scales but is not enough at atomic and subatomic scales. Quantum mechanics handles many systems that classical physics cannot describe, and classical mechanics can be derived from it as an approximation that holds at ordinary scales.

paragraphs.heading: How it began
paragraphs.text: The theory grew gradually out of attempts to explain observations that classical physics could not. Two of these were Max Planck's 1900 solution to the black-body radiation problem and Albert Einstein's 1905 paper on the photoelectric effect, which tied energy to frequency. These early efforts, now called the old quantum theory, led to full quantum mechanics in the mid-1920s. Niels Bohr, Erwin Schrödinger, Werner Heisenberg, Max Born and Paul Dirac were among those who built it. Its ideas are now used in quantum chemistry, quantum biology, quantum technology and quantum information science.

paragraphs.heading: Strange rules
paragraphs.text: In a quantum system, bound states are quantized: energy, momentum and similar quantities can take only certain separate values. In classical systems, by contrast, these quantities can be measured continuously. Measurements of quantum systems show features of both particles and waves, which is called wave–particle duality. There is also a limit to how accurately a quantity can be predicted before it is measured, even when all the starting conditions are known; this is the uncertainty principle.

paragraphs.heading: Only probabilities
paragraphs.text: The theory usually cannot say for certain what will happen; it gives probabilities. An electron, for example, can be described by a wave function, which gives every point in space a complex number called a probability amplitude. Taking the square of the absolute value of that number gives a probability, a recipe called the Born rule after Max Born. Applied to the electron, it gives the chances of finding it at each position when you measure it. That is the best the theory can do.

paragraphs.heading: Interference and tunnelling
paragraphs.text: Quantum interference is often illustrated with the double-slit experiment. Light passing two parallel slits makes bright and dark bands on a screen, yet it always arrives at separate points, like particles. If you detect which slit each particle goes through, the bands do not form, and electrons, atoms and molecules behave the same way. Another effect is quantum tunnelling: a particle can cross a barrier even when its kinetic energy is lower than the barrier's peak, where in classical mechanics it would be trapped. Tunnelling makes radioactive decay and nuclear fusion in stars possible, and it is used in scanning tunnelling microscopes.

paragraphs.heading: Entanglement
paragraphs.text: When quantum systems interact, they can become entangled: their properties are so intertwined that the whole can no longer be described just by its separate parts. Entanglement enables quantum computing and is part of quantum key distribution. Despite a popular misconception, it does not allow signals to be sent faster than light. Results led by Bell's theorem, and many Bell tests, have shown that broad classes of "hidden variable" theories do not fit with quantum physics.

paragraphs.heading: Tested to high precision
paragraphs.text: Experiments have confirmed the predictions of quantum mechanics to an extremely high degree of accuracy. Quantum electrodynamics, the refinement that covers how light and matter interact, agrees with experiment to within 1 part in 10¹² when it predicts the magnetic properties of an electron.
